title: “YOUR BODY IS A TEMPLE”—BUT PAUL WASN’T TALKING ABOUT YOUR WEIGHT, YOUR WORKOUTS, OR YOUR DIET
paragraphs: “YOUR BODY IS A TEMPLE”—BUT PAUL WASN’T TALKING ABOUT YOUR WEIGHT, YOUR WORKOUTS, OR YOUR DIET

The terrifying truth behind one of Christianity’s most quoted—and misunderstood—Bible verses. What God actually said about your body, the secret battles nobody sees, and the scandalous grace of Jesus Christ that can change everything.
There is something deeply unsettling about a Bible verse that we have heard our entire lives… only to discover that we may have missed the very warning God was giving us.
You have probably heard it.
“Your body is a temple.”
Maybe someone said it while encouraging you to exercise.
Maybe you heard it during a conversation about smoking, alcohol, healthy eating, or getting enough sleep.
Maybe you have even repeated it yourself while looking in the mirror, promising to take better care of the body God gave you.
And caring for your health is certainly worthwhile.
But what if I told you that when the apostle Paul wrote those words, he was confronting something far more serious than an unhealthy lifestyle?

What if the original passage had less to do with the food on your plate and much more to do with what happens when a person who belongs to Jesus begins treating their body as though it belongs to nobody but themselves?
What if the verse we turned into a motivational quote was actually a holy confrontation with sexual sin, divided loyalties, and the astonishing price of our redemption?
And what if, buried inside that confrontation, there was also a message of grace powerful enough to reach the person who feels too ashamed to enter a church?
Because here is the part many people never hear.
Paul was not merely telling Christians to respect their bodies.
He was reminding them that their bodies had been purchased by the blood of Jesus Christ.
And once you understand what that means, those familiar words will never sound the same again.
In 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, Paul writes:
That is the King James Version.
Read it again.
Not because it is complicated.
But because we have become so familiar with its words that we sometimes fail to feel their weight.
“Ye are not your own.”
Imagine hearing that in a culture where personal freedom is often treated as the highest good.
My body.
My desires.
My decisions.
My truth.
My life.
And then Scripture interrupts:
You are not your own.
Not because your body is worthless.
But because, in Christ, you have been redeemed at a cost beyond anything money could ever purchase.
Before we go further, we need to return to Corinth.
Because context changes everything.
Corinth was a prosperous, influential city in the Roman world. It was a place of commerce, status, religious diversity, and competing moral expectations.
And the church planted there was struggling.
These were people who had heard the Gospel.
Some had come out of deeply sinful lifestyles.
They had been introduced to the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
But conversion did not instantly erase every habit, temptation, cultural assumption, or destructive pattern they had brought with them.
Does that sound familiar?
You love Jesus.
You believe His Word.
You know what He has delivered you from.
But there are still moments when the person you used to be seems to whisper louder than the person you are becoming.
There are battles you fight privately that nobody at church knows about.
There are thoughts you would be embarrassed to say aloud.
There are temptations that seem to arrive precisely when you are tired, lonely, disappointed, angry, or spiritually exhausted.
And sometimes the most frightening part is not that temptation exists.
It is how easily the human heart can begin negotiating with something God has already called sin.
That was part of the crisis Paul was addressing.
In 1 Corinthians 6:12, he writes:
Paul appears to be responding to a slogan about freedom that some Corinthians were using or misusing.
His answer was devastatingly clear.
Not everything people claim as freedom is beneficial.
And anything that gains mastery over you deserves serious examination.
Then, in verse 13, Paul turns directly toward the body and sexual immorality.
“Now the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body.”
There it is.
The immediate subject is not calorie intake.
It is not muscle development.
It is not a fitness routine.
It is sexual immorality and the theological meaning of the human body.
The Greek word translated “fornication” in the King James Version is πορνεία (porneia), a broad term referring to sexual immorality.
Paul was confronting the idea that what someone does sexually with their body can somehow be separated from their relationship with Christ.
And he would not allow that separation.
Because the Gospel does not merely claim the religious part of your life.
Jesus is Lord over the whole person.
Your thoughts matter.
Your choices matter.
Your relationships matter.
And yes, what you do with your body matters.
But notice something essential.
Paul does not build his argument on the claim that the physical body is dirty or spiritually inferior.
He builds it on the exact opposite truth.
The body matters so much to God that He will raise it.
In 1 Corinthians 6:14, Paul declares:
“And God hath both raised up the Lord, and will also raise up us by his own power.”
Think about that.
Christianity does not teach that salvation is merely the escape of a soul from a worthless physical shell.
The resurrection of Jesus Christ announces that God has not abandoned His purpose for embodied human life.
The same God who raised Jesus from the dead has promised resurrection to those who belong to Christ.
Your body is not an accidental container for your spiritual existence.
It is part of the person God created and intends to redeem.
This is why Paul takes sexual sin so seriously.
In verse 15, he asks:
“Know ye not that your bodies are the members of Christ?”
Then he confronts the unthinkable possibility of taking what belongs to Christ and joining it to sexual immorality.
He even refers specifically to union with a prostitute.
The point is not that one kind of sinner is beyond redemption.
The point is that union with Christ is not a casual religious label.
It is a sacred reality.
And sexual union is not morally meaningless simply because a culture has decided to treat it that way.
Paul appeals to Genesis 2:24, the biblical description of two becoming one flesh.
Then he writes in 1 Corinthians 6:17:
Do you see the contrast?
The Corinthians were being tempted to treat sexual activity as something spiritually insignificant.
Paul reminded them that belonging to Christ changes how they must understand their bodies.
And now we arrive at the command that many Christians desperately need to hear again.
“Flee fornication.”
First Corinthians 6:18.
Not entertain it.
Not secretly manage it.
Not see how close you can get before crossing the line.
Flee.
The Greek word is φεύγετε (pheugete), a present imperative from the verb pheugō, meaning to flee or escape.
The command carries urgency.
It calls for decisive action, not casual negotiation.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly why that matters.
Because you did not always intend to go as far as you went.
It began with a conversation.
A message.
A secret account.
A photograph.
A friendship that slowly became emotionally intimate in ways it should not have.
A private habit you kept promising to stop.
A relationship you knew was pulling you away from obedience to Christ.
At first, your conscience was loud.
Then the excuses became easier.
Then the boundaries moved.
And eventually you found yourself doing something you once believed you would never do.
Maybe you still pray.
Maybe you still worship.
Maybe you still tell people that Jesus is the answer.
But there is a part of your life you have been carefully keeping out of sight.
And when you hear the words “your body is a temple,” you feel something that no fitness advice could ever touch.
Conviction.
Not because God despises your body.
But because He loves you too much to pretend that what is destroying you is harmless.
Yet before shame convinces you to close this article, there is something you need to understand.
Conviction is not the same as condemnation.
The Holy Spirit does not expose sin because Jesus has run out of mercy.
God's Word exposes sin so that we will stop hiding from the Savior who came to rescue sinners.
And that distinction matters more than you may realize.
Because shame often says, “You are what you have done.”
But the Gospel announces that Jesus Christ can forgive, cleanse, and transform those who repent and believe in Him.
Some people reading this have carried secret guilt for years.
Some were introduced to sexual experiences before they were old enough to understand what was happening.
Some were exploited, manipulated, or abused.
If that describes you, hear this clearly.
What someone else did to you was not your sin.
You are not spiritually defiled because someone violated you.
You do not need to repent for being harmed.
And nothing in Paul's teaching gives anyone permission to blame victims, excuse abusers, or pressure wounded people into silence.
God sees what happened.
He is not indifferent to injustice.
And the invitation to healing is not a demand that you pretend the wound never existed.
For others, the burden is different.
You know you made the choice.
You knew the boundary.
You heard the warning.
And you crossed it anyway.
You cannot blame another person for everything.
You cannot rewrite what happened.
You cannot make sin holy simply by attaching a beautiful explanation to it.
But you can come to Jesus.
Not with a polished performance.
Not with a promise that your own strength will never fail again.
With repentance.
With faith.
With an honest confession that you need the mercy and transforming power of God.
And this is where the entire passage becomes even more breathtaking.
Paul says:
“What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?”
The Greek phrase behind “your body is a temple” includes:
τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν
to sōma hymōn naos tou en hymin hagiou pneumatos estin
In context, it means that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you.
Pay attention to the word ναός (naos).
Greek had words that could refer broadly to a temple complex, but naos especially refers to the temple sanctuary, the sacred dwelling place associated with divine presence.
Paul is not casually comparing your body to a religious building.
He is describing the astonishing reality of the Holy Spirit dwelling in believers.
And that is where the metaphor becomes overwhelming.
Under the old covenant, the tabernacle and later the temple represented God's dwelling among His people.
The innermost sanctuary, the Most Holy Place, was associated with His holy presence.
Access was restricted.
The sacrificial system continually reminded Israel that a holy God cannot be approached carelessly by sinful humanity.
Then Jesus came.
The eternal Son of God took on flesh.
He lived without sin.
He died for sinners.
And when He gave up His life, the temple veil was torn.
Matthew 27:51 records that extraordinary event.
The book of Hebrews explains that through the blood of Jesus, believers now have confidence to draw near to God.
Not because holiness no longer matters.
But because Christ has opened the way.
And now Paul tells believers that the Holy Spirit dwells in them.
Not as a reward for having achieved physical perfection.
Not because they have flawless bodies.
Not because they have never struggled.
But because they belong to Christ.
There is another detail that makes this passage even more powerful.
In the Greek text, the word translated “your” in “your body” is plural, while “body” is singular.
Paul is addressing believers together, even while speaking about their bodily conduct.
That means we must not isolate this verse from the communal life of the church.
In 1 Corinthians 3:16–17, Paul has already described the church collectively as God's temple, warning against those who destroy God's people.
Here in chapter 6, he applies temple language to bodily holiness in the context of sexual conduct.
Both dimensions matter.
The Christian body is not disposable.
And the Christian community is not a place where people should be exploited, dishonored, or treated as objects.
The Spirit's presence calls us to holiness in private and to love, justice, and integrity in community.
Imagine what would happen if we took that seriously.

Imagine if we stopped using “your body is a temple” primarily to embarrass people about their appearance and started allowing it to confront the ways we use, exploit, objectify, or dishonor human beings.
Imagine if a husband remembered that his wife is not an object for his selfish desires.
Imagine if a wife remembered that her worth is not determined by whether she can maintain the appearance she had twenty years ago.
Imagine if young men and women were taught that purity is not merely about protecting a reputation but about honoring Christ.
Imagine if churches became places where people struggling with pornography, sexual temptation, betrayal, and shame could seek biblical accountability without being publicly humiliated.
Imagine if survivors of abuse found protection instead of suspicion.
Imagine if repentance was preached without compromising grace, and grace was offered without pretending that sin is harmless.
That would be a church taking the holiness of God seriously.
And perhaps that is why this verse feels so different when we read it in context.
It is not asking whether your body looks impressive.
It is asking whether your life honors the One who redeemed you.
Paul then gives the reason.
“For ye are bought with a price.”
In Greek:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς
ēgorasthēte gar timēs
The meaning is straightforward:
“For you were bought with a price.”
The verb ἠγοράσθητε (ēgorasthēte) is a passive form of agorazō, meaning “to buy” or “purchase.”
Paul is using the language of purchase to communicate the profound reality of belonging to God through redemption.
But what was the price?
First Peter 1:18–19 tells believers that they were not redeemed with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
The price was not your church attendance.
It was not your charitable giving.
It was not your religious performance.
It was not your ability to conquer every temptation by sheer determination.
It was the sacrificial death of Jesus Christ.
The sinless Savior gave Himself for sinners.
And suddenly the temple passage becomes something far deeper than a command to improve your lifestyle.
It becomes a declaration of costly grace.
Jesus did not die merely to make you feel better about yourself.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
To forgive.
To cleanse.
To redeem.
To make people who once lived in rebellion into people who belong to Him.
And because we belong to Him, grace does not leave us unchanged.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains us to reject ungodliness and live in a godly way.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
It is God's undeserved favor that brings salvation and teaches us a new way to live.
But here is a question that deserves to be asked.
What happens when a Christian falls?
What happens when the person who sincerely loves Jesus gives in to temptation again?
What happens when repentance is followed by another battle, another moment of weakness, another painful realization that sanctification is not always a straight line?
Does the Holy Spirit immediately abandon every struggling believer?
Does one failure mean the cross has lost its power?
Does a painful relapse prove that genuine restoration is impossible?
Scripture does not teach us to treat sin lightly.
But neither does it teach believers to despair of the mercy of Christ.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
And First John 2:1 points believers to Jesus Christ the righteous as our advocate with the Father.
That is not an invitation to plan tomorrow's sin.
It is an invitation to stop hiding today's sin.
There is a difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and deciding that obedience no longer matters.
There is a difference between genuine repentance and merely regretting that someone discovered what you did.
And God knows the difference.
He sees what people cannot see.
He knows whether you are bringing your darkness into His light or simply looking for religious language to keep it hidden.
But He also knows how weak you are.
He remembers that you are dust.
And He has not called you to overcome the flesh apart from the power of His Spirit.
This is why the Christian life cannot be reduced to behavior modification.
You can delete an app and still have a heart full of lust.
You can end an unhealthy relationship and still crave the attention that drew you into it.
You can change your appearance and still despise yourself.
You can build impressive physical discipline and still live spiritually compromised.
Real transformation requires more than rearranging external habits.
It requires a renewed mind, a surrendered heart, and the ongoing work of the Holy Spirit.
Romans 12:1 urges believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God.
Romans 12:2 calls for transformation through the renewing of the mind.
And Galatians 5:16 tells us to walk in the Spirit rather than fulfill the desires of the flesh.
These passages do not dismiss practical decisions.
Sometimes repentance requires ending a relationship.
Sometimes it means confessing a secret to a trustworthy, spiritually mature person.

Sometimes it requires removing access to temptation, pursuing pastoral accountability, seeking professional help for compulsive patterns, or taking concrete steps to protect someone who has been harmed.
Sometimes it means admitting that your private choices have consequences for other people.
And when sin involves abuse, coercion, exploitation, or criminal wrongdoing, repentance includes taking responsibility and respecting the need for protection, justice, and appropriate reporting.
Grace is never an excuse to avoid accountability.
But none of these actions purchases salvation.
They are responses to God's grace, not substitutes for the finished work of Christ.
And that brings us to another misunderstanding.
Does this mean Christians should not care about health?
Of course not.
The body is God's good creation, and caring for it can be an expression of responsible stewardship.
Rest, nourishment, movement, medical care, and wise habits can serve our ability to love God and others.
First Timothy 4:8 recognizes that bodily training has some value while emphasizing the greater and lasting value of godliness.
But we must be careful not to force 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 to say something it was not primarily written to say.
Paul's immediate concern was sexual immorality and the believer's belonging to Christ.
It was not a command to achieve a particular weight.
It was not a condemnation of people living with disabilities.
It was not a judgment against those suffering chronic illness.
It was not a declaration that the healthiest-looking Christian must also be the holiest.
A person can be physically strong and spiritually rebellious.
Another can be physically weak and deeply faithful.
Your medical condition is not a reliable measurement of your holiness.
Your appearance does not determine whether you are loved by God.
And no amount of exercise can accomplish what only the blood of Jesus can accomplish.
The Gospel is not a body-transformation program.
It is the good news of salvation through Jesus Christ, whose resurrection also gives believers hope for the redemption of their bodies.
And there is something even more personal here.
Perhaps the body you have struggled to accept is the same body through which you have experienced enormous pain.
Perhaps you look in the mirror and see scars.
Perhaps illness has changed what you can do.
Perhaps aging has taken away strength you once took for granted.
Perhaps you have spent years comparing yourself with people who seem healthier, more attractive, or more capable.
And somewhere along the way, you began to believe that you were less valuable.
Please hear what this passage does not say.
It does not say your body must become impressive before God can dwell in you.
It does not say you must erase every scar before you can honor Christ.
It does not say your weakness disqualifies you from His love.
The apostle Paul himself knew physical weakness, suffering, and affliction.
And in 2 Corinthians 12:9, the Lord told him:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
There are people whose bodies cannot do what they once could, yet whose lives display extraordinary faithfulness.
There are people who worship through pain.
People who pray through exhaustion.
People who continue trusting Jesus while carrying burdens others cannot see.
Their bodies are not failed temples because they are suffering.
And their hope rests not in perfect physical health but in the risen Christ.
One day, those who belong to Jesus will be raised.
The brokenness of this present age will not have the final word.
The resurrection will.
But until then, the question remains.
What are we doing with the lives Christ has redeemed?
Because the verse does not end with the announcement that we were purchased.
It ends with a command.
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
The Greek text of 1 Corinthians 6:20 concludes:
δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν
doxasate dē ton theon en tō sōmati hymōn
That is:
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
The command δοξάσατε (doxasate) calls believers to glorify or honor God.
And the word “therefore” is crucial.
We do not glorify God with our bodies so that He will finally agree to redeem us.
We glorify God because, in Christ, we have been redeemed.
Obedience flows from grace.
Holiness is the response of a person who belongs to Jesus.
And that changes the question from “How much can I get away with?” to “How can my life honor the Savior who gave Himself for me?”
It changes how we think about sexual relationships.
It changes how we respond to temptation.
It changes how we treat our spouses.
It changes how we view other people's bodies.
It changes how we care for those who are vulnerable.
It changes how we handle our private habits.
It even changes how we think about our time, resources, and opportunities to serve.
Not because every one of those issues is the direct subject of 1 Corinthians 6.
But because belonging to Christ has implications for the whole Christian life.
And perhaps the most painful question of all is this.
If Jesus paid such a price to redeem us, why do we so often live as though our deepest desires have the final authority?
That question should humble every one of us.
The preacher.
The worship leader.
The longtime believer.
The new convert.
The person who seems spiritually strong.
The person who is barely holding on.
None of us has outgrown our need for grace.
None of us can stand before God and claim that we have earned His mercy.
We all need Jesus.
And this is where I want you to remember a woman from the Gospel of John.
A woman brought before Jesus after being caught in adultery.
Her accusers wanted condemnation.
They used her shame as a weapon.
They placed her in the middle of a crowd and demanded a judgment.
And Jesus confronted the hypocrisy of those who were ready to condemn her.
One by one, her accusers departed.
Then Jesus spoke words that have comforted broken sinners for generations.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
John 8:11.

There is a textual detail worth knowing: the account in John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel, and modern Bible editions commonly note this. Its themes of mercy and repentance are nevertheless taught clearly elsewhere in Scripture.
And notice the two truths held together in this account.
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin behind.
Jesus did not tell the woman that adultery was harmless.
But neither did He join the crowd in using her humiliation for entertainment.
He confronted sin without abandoning compassion.
He offered mercy without celebrating rebellion.
That is the balance we desperately need.
Some churches speak about holiness in ways that make wounded people afraid to seek help.
Others speak about grace in ways that make repentance seem unnecessary.
But biblical Christianity refuses both distortions.
Jesus receives repentant sinners.
And Jesus calls sinners to follow Him into a transformed life.
This is not scandal being covered with religious language.
This is scandal meeting grace.
And grace leading to change.
Perhaps your scandal was public.
People know what happened.
They know about the betrayal.
The divorce.
The affair.
The addiction.
The secret that became a headline in your family.
Perhaps you are still living with consequences that cannot simply be erased.
Or perhaps your scandal has never been discovered.
Nobody knows what happens when you close your bedroom door.
Nobody knows what you search for.
Nobody knows the messages you delete.
Nobody knows the promises you keep breaking.
Nobody knows how far your heart has wandered.
But God knows.
And the astonishing news of the Gospel is that the God who knows the truth about your sin is the very God who sent His Son to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired our reputations.
Not after we had learned how to sound spiritual.
Not after we had achieved a flawless record.
Christ died for sinners.
And the risen Savior still calls people to repentance and faith.
So if this article has uncovered something you have been hiding, do not turn that conviction into another season of self-hatred.
Bring it to Jesus.
Confess honestly.
Turn from what you know is wrong.
Seek the help and accountability you need.
Make amends where appropriate.
Protect those who have been harmed.
And remember that genuine spiritual growth is often lived out through daily surrender, not one dramatic emotional moment.
You may need to fight temptation again tomorrow.
You may need to rebuild trust over time.
You may need to accept consequences.
You may need to learn obedience in places where you once lived carelessly.
But you do not have to pretend that your strength is enough.
Christ is sufficient.
His Word is true.
His Spirit is powerful.
And His grace is not exhausted by the existence of a difficult battle.
If you are reading this with tears in your eyes, perhaps this is the moment to stop running.
Not because a social media article can save you.
Only Jesus saves.
But the truth of Scripture can point you to the One who can.
And maybe, for the first time in a long time, you are ready to pray something honest.

“Lord Jesus, I have treated parts of my life as though they did not belong to You. I have excused things I should have confessed. I have hidden what I should have brought into Your light. Forgive me. Cleanse me. Teach me to walk in Your truth. Give me the courage to repent, the humility to seek help, and the strength to obey through Your Spirit. I cannot save myself. My hope is in Your death and resurrection. I surrender myself to You. Amen.”
And if that prayer reflects the cry of your heart, do not let the moment end with emotion alone.
Open your Bible.
Return to 1 Corinthians 6.
Read the whole chapter.
Read Romans 6.
Read Psalm 51.
Read First John 1.
Speak with a trustworthy, biblically grounded Christian who can walk with you.
Find a faithful local church where Scripture is taught, Christ is exalted, and accountability is practiced with compassion and integrity.
And if you are still struggling, do not confuse the length of the battle with proof that God cannot help you.
Keep coming into the light.
Keep clinging to Christ.
Keep taking the next faithful step.
Because there is another person who needs to read this.
Someone who has been told that Christianity is only about looking respectable.
Someone who believes their past has made them permanently unworthy.
Someone who has spent years confusing a healthy appearance with a holy life.
Someone who is trapped in secret sin and does not know how to ask for help.
Someone who needs to discover that the command to glorify God with their body is rooted in the extraordinary grace of being redeemed by Jesus Christ.
Not merely to increase the number of people who see it.
But because someone in your family, your church, or your circle of friends may be silently wrestling with the very truth we have explored.
One thoughtful share can open a conversation that someone has been afraid to begin.

And if a particular person comes to mind, consider tagging them with kindness and discretion—never to expose their private struggles, but to invite them into a conversation about Scripture, grace, and hope.
And I want to invite you to do something more personal.
You do not need to describe private sins or reveal painful details publicly.
Sometimes the most courageous testimony is simply admitting that you still need Jesus.
And if this message challenged an assumption you had about the phrase “your body is a temple,” tell us what you learned.
Your honest reflection may help someone else open their Bible and discover the passage for themselves.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a following around a personality.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to make people dependent on a page.
But to keep pointing hearts back to the authority of Scripture, the sufficiency of Jesus Christ, the necessity of repentance, and the hope of the Gospel.
And invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe in Jesus to follow as well.
Because the next article may be the one that helps someone understand a biblical truth they have never been taught.
The next devotional may encourage someone who is close to giving up.
The next Scripture reflection may challenge someone to return to Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, including to people who may not be able to afford paid materials.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, thoughtfully, and cheerfully, not under pressure or compulsion, as we see in 2 Corinthians 9:7.
It does not purchase His favor.
It does not replace the responsibilities of generosity, stewardship, and support within your local church.
And it is not a condition for glorifying Him.
But if you believe this ministry is serving a worthwhile purpose, supporting it can be one meaningful way to use your resources for the good of others and the spread of biblical truth.
These items are simply an additional way to encourage faith, reflection, and everyday reminders of biblical truth.
They are not the reason the Gospel matters.
Jesus is.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The grace of Jesus Christ cannot be purchased.
We simply want more people to hear the truth that has the power to lead them to the Savior.
Because when all the discussions about temples, bodies, holiness, purity, redemption, and grace are finished, one truth remains.
You were created for more than the temporary satisfaction of whatever desire is loudest today.
You were not made to be ruled by every appetite.
You were not made to live forever beneath the weight of shame.
And you were not made to carry the impossible burden of saving yourself.
Jesus Christ came into a world of broken people.
He lived the righteous life we could not live.
He bore the penalty of sin through His sacrificial death.
He rose again in victory.
And He calls sinners to turn to Him in repentance and faith.
That is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement dressed in religious language.
Not a promise that Christians will never struggle.
Not a guarantee of perfect health, effortless success, or a life without suffering.
It is the announcement that forgiveness and reconciliation with God are found in Jesus Christ.
And because He lives, those who belong to Him have a living hope.
So the next time someone says, “Your body is a temple,” remember Corinth.
Remember Paul's warning.
Remember the Holy Spirit.
Remember the resurrection.
Remember the price.
And above all, remember the Savior.
The One who did not merely tell sinners to clean themselves up.
The One who gave Himself to redeem them.
The One whose grace calls us out of darkness and into a new life.
You may have treated your body carelessly.
You may have dishonored God through choices you deeply regret.
You may still be learning what surrender looks like.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your past does not have the authority to cancel what His blood has accomplished.
And if you have not yet come to Him, His invitation to repent and believe the Gospel is still before you.
The call is serious.
The cost of redemption was immeasurable.
And the grace of God is more astonishing than we often dare to imagine.
The body you once used to hide your shame can become the very place where your life bears witness to the grace of the Savior who redeemed you.
